A.q: Which set lists only functions of the skeletal system?
options: Producing body heat, generating locomotion, and contracting to move the limbs
Storing minerals, forming blood cells, and providing a surface for muscle attachment
Filtering lymph, housing immune cells, and removing foreign particles from tissue fluid
Exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide, regulating blood pressure, and adjusting heart rate
A.explain: The skeletal system stores minerals, performs hemopoiesis (blood cell formation), and provides a surface for muscle attachment, so the set that names mineral storage, blood-cell formation, and a muscle-attachment surface is the skeletal set. Producing body heat, generating locomotion, and contracting to move the limbs are functions of muscle. Filtering lymph, housing immune cells, and removing foreign particles are functions of the lymphatic system. Exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide, regulating blood pressure, and adjusting heart rate are functions of the respiratory and cardiovascular systems.

A.q: Which pairing of a directional term with its point of reference is correct?
options: Proximal marks a point that lies away from the origin or beginning of a structure.
Distal marks a point that lies near the origin or beginning of a structure.
Medial marks a position that lies close to the imaginary midline running down the body.
Lateral marks a position that lies close to the imaginary midline running down the body.
A.explain: Medial means close to the midline, so the pairing that places medial close to the imaginary midline is correct. Proximal means near the origin or beginning of a structure, not away from it, so the line that places proximal away from the origin reverses the term. Distal means away from the origin, not near it, so the line that places distal near the origin reverses that pair. Lateral means toward the side, away from the midline, so the line that places lateral close to the midline assigns the medial sense to lateral.

A.q: Which pairing of anterior, posterior, superior, or inferior with its point of reference is correct?
options: Anterior refers to the back or dorsal side of the body, and posterior refers to the front or ventral side.
Superior means away from the head, and inferior means toward the head.
Anterior refers to the front or ventral side of the body, and posterior refers to the back or dorsal side.
Superior means toward the side, and inferior means toward the midline.
A.explain: Anterior refers to the front or ventral side, and posterior refers to the back or dorsal side, so that pairing is correct. The line that assigns anterior to the back or dorsal side and posterior to the front or ventral side reverses the two. Superior means toward the head and inferior means away from the head, so the line that sends superior away from the head and inferior toward the head reverses the vertical pair. The line that sends superior toward the side and inferior toward the midline confuses the vertical pair with lateral and medial.

A.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes compact bone from spongy (cancellous) bone?
options: Compact bone is tight and solid and forms the exterior of bones, while spongy bone is mesh-like and forms the interior around the medullary cavity.
Compact bone is mesh-like and forms the interior around the medullary cavity, while spongy bone is tight and solid and forms the exterior of bones.
Compact bone stores the blood cells held in the medullary cavity, while spongy bone provides the principal surface for muscle attachment.
Compact bone produces the blood components directly, while spongy bone supplies the lubricating gristle at the joints.
A.explain: Compact bone is the tight, solid tissue that makes up the exterior of bones, and spongy (cancellous) bone is the mesh-like tissue that fills the interior and surrounds the medullary cavity, so that contrast is correct. The line that calls compact bone mesh-like and interior, and spongy bone tight and exterior, reverses the two tissues. Blood-cell storage belongs to marrow rather than to a compact-versus-spongy contrast, and the attachment surface is a general property of bone, so the line about storing blood cells and providing the attachment surface misattributes both roles. Lubrication at the joints is the job of articular cartilage, not of spongy bone, so the line about producing blood components and supplying lubricating gristle is wrong on both points.

A.q: Regarding red and yellow bone marrow, which statement is correct?
options: Yellow marrow produces the red cells, white cells, and platelets, while red marrow is the tissue that stores fat.
At birth all human marrow is yellow, and red tissue gradually replaces some of it as a person matures into adulthood.
Red marrow produces the blood components, and at birth all marrow is red, after which fat tissue converts part of it to yellow.
Red marrow is responsible for producing fats, cartilages, and bone, while yellow marrow performs the formation of blood cells.
A.explain: Red marrow forms the blood components (red cells, white cells, and platelets), and because the demand for new blood is high at birth all marrow starts red, after which fat tissue gradually replaces some of it with yellow marrow. The line that assigns blood-cell production to yellow marrow and fat storage to red marrow swaps the products. The line that starts all marrow as yellow and then replaces it with red reverses the age change, since red is the starting tissue and yellow the later replacement. The line that assigns fat, cartilage, and bone production to red marrow and blood formation to yellow marrow swaps the roles again.

A.q: Fibrocartilage and articular cartilage are both gristle tissues but serve different roles. Which assignment of role to tissue is correct?
options: Fibrocartilage lubricates the bone surfaces for articulation, while articular cartilage attaches bone to bone with restricted mobility at the joints.
Fibrocartilage attaches bone to other bones and limits joint mobility, while articular cartilage lubricates the surfaces for articulation.
Both fibrocartilage and articular cartilage generate the red and white blood cells found within the medullary cavity.
Both fibrocartilage and articular cartilage store the minerals that give the skeleton its overall shape and support.
A.explain: Articular cartilage is the gristle-like lubricating layer on bone surfaces where they articulate, and fibrocartilage binds bone to bone while allowing only restricted movement at the joint, so the assignment of limited mobility to fibrocartilage and lubrication to articular cartilage is correct. The line that gives lubrication to fibrocartilage and bone-to-bone attachment to articular cartilage swaps the two. Blood-cell formation is the work of red marrow, not of either cartilage, so the line that assigns both tissues to generation of red and white cells is wrong. Mineral storage and the shaping of the skeleton are properties of bone, not of the two cartilages, so the line about storing minerals misstates their role.

A.q: Which function belongs to the muscular system rather than to the skeletal system?
options: Storing minerals within the tissue of the skeleton
Providing the surface to which muscles attach
Performing hemopoiesis within the red marrow
A.explain: Producing body heat through contraction is a function of muscle activity, so it belongs to the muscular system and is the correct choice. Storing minerals is a skeletal role, since bone is a mineral reservoir. Providing the attachment surface is precisely what bone does for muscle, so it is skeletal. Hemopoiesis, the formation of blood cells, occurs in red bone marrow and is therefore skeletal as well. Note that protecting internal organs is shared by both systems and so cannot separate them.

A.q: Which plane divides the body vertically into front (anterior) and back (posterior) portions?
A.explain: The coronal or frontal plane is the vertical plane that divides the body into front (anterior) and back (posterior) portions. The sagittal plane divides the body into right and left portions, the transverse plane divides it into upper and lower portions, and the oblique plane divides it at an angle.

A.q: Which plane divides the body vertically into right and left portions?
A.explain: The sagittal or median plane is the vertical plane that divides the body into right and left portions. The coronal plane divides the body into front and back portions, the transverse plane divides it into upper and lower portions, and the oblique plane divides it at an angle.

A.q: Which plane divides the body horizontally into upper and lower portions?
A.explain: The transverse or horizontal plane is the plane that divides the body into upper and lower portions. The coronal plane divides the body into front and back portions, the sagittal plane divides it into right and left portions, and the oblique plane divides it at an angle.

A.q: Which cell type is the specialized connective tissue cell that forms the skeleton?
A.explain: The osteocyte is the specialized connective tissue cell that forms the skeleton. The chondrocyte is a cartilage cell, the myocyte is a muscle cell, and the fibroblast is a connective tissue cell of fibers rather than of bone.

A.q: The pectoral and pelvic girdles share which structural feature?
options: Both are ball and socket joints encircling bone to support the limbs.
Both are flat bones that form the roof and walls of the chest cage.
Both are irregular bones that make up the vertebral column itself.
Both are sesamoid bones embedded in a tendon near a joint.
A.explain: The pectoral and pelvic girdles both consist of ball and socket joints encircling a bony structure that supports the upper and lower limbs, so that shared feature is correct. Flat bones form the roof and walls of the chest cage, as with the ribs and sternum, and do not form either girdle. Irregular bones form the vertebral column and face, not the girdles. Sesamoid bones such as the patella lie near joints, embedded in tendon, but do not form a girdle.

A.q: Which set consists entirely of combining forms that mean muscle?
A.explain: My/o, Myos/o, and Muscul/o are the three interchangeable spellings of the muscle combining form, seen in myoma, myositis, and muscular. Sarc/o, Fibr/o, and Ton/o mean flesh, fiber, and tone or tension, none of which is muscle. Arthr/o and Articul/o mean joint, and Chondr/o means cartilage. Myel/o means bone marrow or spinal cord, Oste/o means bone, and Crani/o means skull.

A.q: Which pair of combining forms both mean joint?
A.explain: Arthr/o and Articul/o both mean joint, as in arthrodynia and articulus. Chondr/o means cartilage and Oste/o means bone; My/o and Muscul/o mean muscle; Spondyl/o and Vertebr/o mean vertebra.

A.q: Which combining form means cartilage or gristle?
A.explain: Chondr/o means cartilage or gristle, as in chondromalacia. Arthr/o means joint, Myel/o means bone marrow or spinal cord, and Oste/o means bone.

A.q: Which pair of combining forms both mean vertebra?
A.explain: Spondyl/o and Vertebr/o both mean vertebra, as in spondylosis and vertebroplasty. Arthr/o and Articul/o mean joint, Cost/o and Stern/o mean rib and sternum, and Radi/o and Uln/o mean radius and ulna.

A.q: Which set consists entirely of combining forms that mean tendon?
A.explain: Ten/o, Tend/o, and Tendin/o are the three combining forms that mean tendon, as in tenotomy and tendinitis. My/o, Myos/o, and Muscul/o mean muscle; Sarc/o means flesh and Fibr/o means fiber; Arthr/o and Articul/o mean joint and Chondr/o means cartilage.

A.q: Myel/o, Sarc/o, Fibr/o, and Ton/o are easily transposed. Which pairing of form to meaning is correct?
options: Myel/o means flesh, and Sarc/o means the bone marrow of the spinal cord.
Fibr/o means tone or tension, and Ton/o means the fiber of connective tissue.
Sarc/o means fiber, and Fibr/o means the tone or tension of a muscle.
Myel/o means the bone marrow of the spinal cord, and Sarc/o means flesh.
A.explain: Myel/o denotes bone marrow or the spinal cord and Sarc/o denotes flesh, as in myeloma and sarcoma, so that pairing is correct. The line that assigns flesh to Myel/o and bone marrow of the spinal cord to Sarc/o swaps these two senses. Fibr/o means fiber and Ton/o means tone or tension, so the line that assigns tone or tension to Fibr/o and fiber to Ton/o reverses that pair. The line that assigns fiber to Sarc/o and tone or tension to Fibr/o mixes two unrelated forms.

A.q: In the term myeloma, the element myel refers to what?
options: The bone marrow or spinal cord
A.explain: Myel denotes bone marrow or the spinal cord, so the myel element names the tissue in myeloma, a tumor of the bone marrow. The tumor or neoplastic-mass sense in the same word comes from the suffix -oma, not from myel. Flesh is Sarc/o, as in sarcoma, and muscle is My/o or Muscul/o, neither of which is present here. Reading myel as the tumor confuses the combining form with the suffix that follows it.

A.q: In the term sarcoma, the element sarc refers to what?
A.explain: Sarc means flesh, so sarcoma denotes a tumor of fleshy or soft tissue. Bone marrow is Myel/o, cartilage is Chondr/o, and tendon is Ten/o or Tendin/o.

A.q: The term cervicobrachial joins two combining forms. Which pair of regions does it relate?
options: The chest and the lower back
A.explain: Cervicobrachial is built from Cervic/o (neck) and Brachi/o (arm), so it relates the neck and the arm, as in the cervicobrachial region or the nerves of the brachial plexus emerging from the neck. Rib and skull would need Cost/o and Crani/o. Chest and lower back would need Thorac/o and Lumb/o. Hip and femur would need Pelv/o and Femor/o. None of those forms is present in cervicobrachial.

A.q: In the term thoracolumbar, the element thorac refers to which region?
A.explain: Thorac (and its variant Thoracic) means chest, so the thorac element in thoracolumbar names the chest region, while the lumbar element names the lower back. Lower back is the sense of Lumb/o, the other half of the same word, not of thorac. Neck is Cervic/o and hip is Pelv/o, neither of which appears here. Reading thorac as lower back would swap the two regions the compound joins.

A.q: In the term intercostal, the element cost refers to what?
A.explain: Cost means rib, so intercostal denotes a position between the ribs. Sternum is Stern/o, vertebra is Spondyl/o or Vertebr/o, and skull is Crani/o.

A.q: What does the term craniotomy mean?
options: Surgical removal of a portion of the skull.
A.explain: Craniotomy is built from Crani/o (skull) and -tomy (incision), so it denotes incision into the skull. Surgical removal would use -ectomy, inflammation would use -itis, and a record would use -gram.

A.q: What does the term dactylitis mean?
A.explain: Dactylitis is built from Dactyl/o (digit) and -itis (inflammation), so it denotes inflammation of a digit. Pain would use -dynia, surgical repair would use -plasty, and a record would use -gram.

A.q: What does the term chondromalacia mean?
A.explain: Chondromalacia is built from Chondr/o (cartilage) and -malacia (softening), so it denotes softening of cartilage. Inflammation would use -itis, surgical removal would use -ectomy, and a tumor would use -oma.

A.q: What does the term arthrodynia mean?
A.explain: Arthrodynia is built from Arthr/o (joint) and -dynia (pain), so it denotes pain in a joint. Inflammation would use -itis, surgical repair would use -plasty, and a record would use -gram.

A.q: What does the term osteoarthrotomy mean?
options: Incision into a bone and a joint.
Inflammation of a bone and a joint.
A record of a bone and a joint.
Softening of a bone and a joint.
A.explain: Osteoarthrotomy is built from Oste/o (bone), Arthr/o (joint), and -tomy (incision), so it denotes incision into a bone and a joint. Inflammation would use -itis, a record would use -gram, and softening would use -malacia.

A.q: What does the term spondylosis mean?
options: A stiff, immobile condition of vertebrae.
Surgical removal of a vertebral bone.
A tumor arising in a vertebral bone.
A.explain: Spondylosis is built from Spondyl/o (vertebra) and -osis (condition), so it denotes a condition of stiff and immobile vertebrae. Inflammation would use -itis, surgical removal would use -ectomy, and a tumor would use -oma.

A.q: What does the term tenotomy mean?
A.explain: Tenotomy is built from Ten/o (tendon) and -tomy (incision), so it denotes incision into a tendon. Surgical removal would use -ectomy, inflammation would use -itis, and a record would use -gram.

A.q: What does the term tendinitis mean?
A.explain: Tendinitis is built from Tendin/o (tendon) and -itis (inflammation), so it denotes inflammation of a tendon, as in wrist tendinitis. Pain would use -dynia, surgical repair would use -plasty, and a tumor would use -oma.

A.q: What does the term dystonia mean?
A.explain: Dystonia is built from the prefix dys- (abnormal) and Ton/o (tone or tension) with -ia (condition), so it denotes abnormal tone or tension, usually of muscle. Pain would use -dynia, inflammation would use -itis, and a tumor would use -oma.

A.q: What does the term pelvimetry mean?
A.explain: Pelvimetry is built from Pelv/i (pelvis) and -metry (measurement), so it denotes measurement of the pelvis. A record would use -gram, inflammation would use -itis, and surgical repair would use -plasty.

A.q: What does the term pelvofemoral mean?
options: Pertaining to the pelvis and the femur.
Pertaining to the pelvis and the sternum.
Pertaining to the pelvis and the skull.
Pertaining to the pelvis and the rib.
A.explain: Pelvofemoral is built from Pelv/o (pelvis) and Femor/o (femur) with -al (pertaining to), so it means pertaining to the pelvis and the femur. The sternum, skull, and rib are named by Stern/o, Crani/o, and Cost/o, none of which appears here.

A.q: What does the term radioulnar mean?
options: Pertaining to the radius and the ulna.
Pertaining to the ribs and the sternum.
Pertaining to the femur and the tibia.
Pertaining to the carpal and the tarsal bones.
A.explain: Radioulnar is built from Radi/o (radius) and Uln/o (ulna) with -ar (pertaining to), so it means pertaining to the radius and the ulna. The ribs and sternum are Cost/o and Stern/o, the femur and tibia are Femor/o and Tibi/o, and the carpal and tarsal bones are Carp/o and Tars/o.

A.q: What does the term sternocostal mean?
options: Pertaining to the sternum and the ribs.
Pertaining to the sternum and the skull.
Pertaining to the sternum and the pelvis.
Pertaining to the sternum and the vertebra.
A.explain: Sternocostal is built from Stern/o (sternum) and Cost/o (rib) with -al (pertaining to), so it means pertaining to the sternum and the ribs. The skull, pelvis, and vertebra are named by Crani/o, Pelv/o, and Spondyl/o, none of which appears here.

A.q: What does the term myoma mean?
A.explain: Myoma is built from My/o (muscle) and -oma (tumor), so it denotes a tumor of muscle tissue. Inflammation would use -itis (myositis), pain would use -dynia, and softening would use -malacia.

A.q: What does the term myositis mean?
A.explain: Myositis is built from Myos/o (muscle) and -itis (inflammation), so it denotes inflammation of muscle tissue. A tumor would use -oma (myoma), pain would use -dynia, and softening would use -malacia.

A.q: What does the term fibrocartilage mean?
options: Cartilage made of fibrous tissue that attaches bones to other bones.
Cartilage that lubricates the joint surfaces for articulation.
Bone tissue that stores minerals within the skeleton.
Muscle tissue that contracts to produce body heat.
A.explain: Fibrocartilage is built from Fibr/o (fiber) and Chondr/o (cartilage), so it denotes fibrous cartilage, the tissue that attaches bones to other bones and provides restricted mobility to the joints. Lubricating joint surfaces is the role of articular cartilage, mineral storage is a bone function, and heat production is a muscle function.

A.q: What does the term brachioplasty mean?
A.explain: Brachioplasty is built from Brachi/o (arm) and -plasty (surgical repair), so it denotes surgical repair of the arm. Inflammation would use -itis, pain would use -dynia, and a record would use -gram.

A.q: What does the term femoral mean?
A.explain: Femoral is built from Femor/o (femur) and -al (pertaining to), so it means pertaining to the femur. The rib, skull, and vertebra are named by Cost/o, Crani/o, and Spondyl/o.

A.q: What does the term lumbar mean?
options: Pertaining to the loin or lower back.
Pertaining to the chest or thorax.
A.explain: Lumbar is built from Lumb/o (loin or lower back) with -ar (pertaining to), so it means pertaining to the lower back. The chest is Thorac/o, the neck is Cervic/o, and the arm is Brachi/o.

A.q: What does the term fascial mean?
options: Pertaining to fascia, a connective band.
Pertaining to tendon, a muscle cord.
Pertaining to a joint, an articulation.
A.explain: Fascial is built from Fasci/o (fascia or band) with -al (pertaining to), so it means pertaining to a fascia. Tendon is Ten/o, joint is Arthr/o, and muscle is My/o.

A.q: What does the term articulus mean?
A.explain: Articulus comes from Articul/o, which means joint, so it denotes a joint. Cartilage is Chondr/o, tendon is Ten/o, and muscle is My/o.

A.q: What does the term osteocyte mean?
A.explain: Osteocyte is built from Oste/o (bone) and -cyte (cell), so it denotes a cell of bone tissue. Cartilage cells are chondrocytes, muscle cells are myocytes, and tendon cells are tenocytes.

A.q: What does the term medullary cavity mean?
options: The central space within a bone that contains marrow.
The gristle-like covering on the joint surfaces of a bone.
The tight solid tissue forming the exterior of a bone.
The mesh-like tissue filling the interior of a bone.
A.explain: The medullary cavity is the central space within a bone that contains marrow. The gristle-like covering on joint surfaces is articular cartilage, the tight solid exterior tissue is compact bone, and the mesh-like interior tissue is spongy or cancellous bone.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the pectoral girdle?
options: It encircles the upper limb and is formed by ball and socket joints supporting the arm.
It encircles the lower limb and is formed by ball and socket joints supporting the leg.
It forms the roof of the thoracic cage and protects the heart and lungs.
It forms the central axis of the skeleton and supports the skull.
A.explain: The pectoral or shoulder girdle encircles the upper limb and is formed by ball and socket joints that support the arm. The line about encircling the lower limb and supporting the leg describes the pelvic girdle. The line about forming the roof of the thoracic cage and protecting the heart and lungs describes the ribs and sternum. The line about forming the central axis and supporting the skull describes the vertebral column.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the pelvic girdle?
options: It encircles the upper limb and supports the arm.
It encircles the lower limb and supports the leg.
It forms the roof of the thoracic cage.
It forms the U-shaped bone at the base of the tongue.
A.explain: The pelvic girdle encircles the lower limb and is formed by ball and socket joints that support the leg. The line about encircling the upper limb and supporting the arm describes the pectoral girdle. The line about forming the roof of the thoracic cage describes the ribs and sternum. The line about the U-shaped bone at the base of the tongue describes the hyoid.

A.q: Match each combining form to the structure or region it denotes.
A.explain: Arthr/o and Articul/o both mean joint, as in arthrodynia and articulus. Chondr/o means cartilage or gristle, as in chondromalacia. My/o, Myos/o, and Muscul/o all mean muscle, as in myoma, myositis, and muscular. Sarc/o means flesh, as in sarcoma. Fibr/o means fiber, as in fibrocartilage. Ton/o means tone or tension, as in dystonia. The paired forms on the left are synonym spellings or closely related forms, so each left entry maps to a single right entry.

A.q: Match each remaining combining form to the structure or region it denotes.
A.explain: Brachi/o means arm, as in brachioplasty. Cervic/o means neck, as in cervicobrachial. Crani/o means skull, as in craniotomy. Dactyl/o means digit, as in dactylitis. Fasci/o means fascia, the band of connective tissue seen in fascial and in the fascial band around muscle fibers. Femor/o means femur, as in femoral. Each form pairs with exactly one structure, and the example terms show the same pairing in use.

A.q: Match each further combining form to the structure or region it denotes.
A.explain: Cost/o means rib, as in intercostal. Lumb/o means the loin or lower back, as in lumbar and thoracolumbar. Oste/o means bone, as in osteoarthrotomy. Pelv/i and Pelv/o are the two spellings for the hip bone or pelvic cavity, as in pelvimetry and pelvofemoral. Radi/o and Uln/o name the two forearm bones, the radius and the ulna, jointly seen in radioulnar. Stern/o means the sternum or breastbone, as in sternocostal. The paired forms on the left are synonym spellings or a natural anatomical pair, so each left entry maps to a single right entry.

A.q: Match each combining form to the structure or idea it denotes.
A.explain: Myel/o means bone marrow or the spinal cord, as in myeloma and leukomyelopathy. Spondyl/o and Vertebr/o both mean vertebra, as in spondylosis and vertebroplasty. Ten/o, Tend/o, and Tendin/o all mean tendon, as in tenotomy and tendinitis. Thorac/o and Thoracic/o mean chest, as in thoracolumbar and thoracicoabdominal. Orth/o means straight, as in orthopedic. Patell/o means the kneecap, or patella.

A.q: Match each term to its meaning.

rightItems.text: Incision into a bone and a joint.

A.explain: Arthrodynia is pain in a joint, built from Arthr/o and -dynia. Chondromalacia is softening of cartilage, built from Chondr/o and -malacia. Craniotomy is incision into the skull, built from Crani/o and -tomy. Dactylitis is inflammation of a digit, built from Dactyl/o and -itis. Intercostal means between the ribs, built from the prefix inter- and Cost/o. Osteoarthrotomy is incision into a bone and a joint, built from Oste/o, Arthr/o, and -tomy.

A.q: Match each remaining term to its meaning.

rightItems.text: A condition of stiff and immobile vertebrae.
Pertaining to the pelvis and the femur.

A.explain: Spondylosis is a condition of stiff and immobile vertebrae, built from Spondyl/o and -osis. Tenotomy is incision into a tendon, built from Ten/o and -tomy. Tendinitis is inflammation of a tendon, built from Tendin/o and -itis. Dystonia is abnormal tone or tension, built from dys- and Ton/o with -ia. Pelvimetry is measurement of the pelvis, built from Pelv/i and -metry. Pelvofemoral means pertaining to the pelvis and the femur, built from Pelv/o and Femor/o.

A.q: Match each further term to its meaning.

rightItems.text: Pertaining to the sternum and the ribs.
Pertaining to the neck and the arm.
Cartilage made of fibrous tissue that attaches bones to other bones.
Pertaining to the radius and the ulna.

A.explain: Radioulnar means pertaining to the radius and the ulna, built from Radi/o and Uln/o. Sternocostal means pertaining to the sternum and the ribs, built from Stern/o and Cost/o. Myoma is a tumor of muscle tissue, built from My/o and -oma. Myositis is inflammation of muscle tissue, built from Myos/o and -itis. Fibrocartilage is cartilage made of fibrous tissue that attaches bones to other bones, built from Fibr/o and Chondr/o. Cervicobrachial means pertaining to the neck and the arm, built from Cervic/o and Brachi/o.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the thoracic cage?
options: It is part of the appendicular skeleton and forms the pelvic girdle.
It is part of the axial skeleton and encloses the chest, formed by the ribs and sternum.
It is part of the appendicular skeleton and supports the upper limb.
It is part of the axial skeleton and forms the U-shaped bone at the base of the tongue.
A.explain: The thoracic cage is part of the axial skeleton and encloses the chest, being formed by the ribs and sternum. The line that places it in the appendicular skeleton and calls it the pelvic girdle confuses it with the pelvic girdle. The line that places it in the appendicular skeleton and says it supports the upper limb confuses it with the pectoral girdle. The line that calls it the U-shaped bone at the base of the tongue confuses it with the hyoid.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the vertebral column?
options: It is part of the appendicular skeleton and supports the lower limb.
It is part of the axial skeleton and forms the central axis of the body.
It is part of the appendicular skeleton and forms the shoulder girdle.
It is part of the axial skeleton and encloses the chest.
A.explain: The vertebral column is part of the axial skeleton and forms the central axis of the body. The line that places it in the appendicular skeleton as support for the lower limb assigns it to the wrong division. The line that places it in the appendicular skeleton as the shoulder girdle does the same. The line that says it encloses the chest describes the thoracic cage, not the vertebral column.

A.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the hyoid bone from the laryngeal skeleton?
options: The hyoid is the U-shaped bone at the base of the tongue, while the laryngeal skeleton is the cartilaginous framework of the voice box.
The hyoid is the cartilaginous framework of the voice box, while the laryngeal skeleton is the U-shaped bone at the base of the tongue.
The hyoid is the breastbone of the chest, while the laryngeal skeleton is the heel bone of the foot.
The hyoid is the kneecap, while the laryngeal skeleton is the shoulder blade.
A.explain: The hyoid is the U-shaped bone at the base of the tongue, while the laryngeal skeleton is the cartilaginous framework of the voice box (larynx). The line that calls the hyoid the framework of the voice box and the laryngeal skeleton the U-shaped bone swaps the two. The breastbone is the sternum and the heel bone is the calcaneus, so the line about the breastbone and the heel bone names neither structure. The kneecap is the patella and the shoulder blade is the scapula, so the line about the kneecap and the shoulder blade is wrong as well.

A.q: Orth/o and ped/o are joined to build one musculoskeletal term. Which pairing of meanings and term is correct?
options: Orth/o means straight and ped/o means foot, forming orthopedic.
Orth/o means foot and ped/o means straight, forming orthopedic.
Orth/o means bone and ped/o means child, forming orthopedic.
Orth/o means mouth and ped/o means muscle, forming muscular.
A.explain: Orth/o means straight and ped/o means foot, and the two combine to form orthopedic. The line that assigns foot to Orth/o and straight to ped/o swaps the two forms inside the same term. Orth/o does not mean bone, and the foot sense of ped/o is the one used in orthopedic, so the line that pairs bone with child misses the straight sense and the foot sense. Mouth and muscle are not the senses of Orth/o and ped/o, and muscular is built from muscul/o, not from this pair.

A.q: What does the term myalgia mean?
A.explain: Myalgia is built from My/o (muscle) and -algia (pain), so it denotes pain in a muscle. Pain in a bone would use Oste/o, as in ostealgia. Inflammation of a muscle is myositis, built with -itis. Softening of a muscle would use -malacia, not -algia.

A.q: Which pairing names the breastbone and the combining form used to build terms for it?
options: Sternum, built with the combining form stern/o.
Chest wall, built with the combining form thorac/o.
Forearm bone, built with the combining form uln/o.
Upper arm, built with the combining form brachi/o.
A.explain: The breastbone is the sternum, and terms for it are built with stern/o, as in sternocostal and sternalgia. Thorac/o names the chest, not the breastbone itself. Uln/o names the ulna, a forearm bone. Brachi/o names the arm, not the breastbone.

A.q: Which term marks the end of a limb farthest from its point of origin?
options: Distal, away from the origin of the structure.
Proximal, near the origin of the structure.
Medial, close to the midline of the body.
Lateral, toward the side and away from midline.
A.explain: Distal marks a point away from the origin or beginning of a structure, so it is the end farthest from that origin. Proximal is the opposite: near the origin, not farthest from it. Medial means close to the midline and does not measure distance from an origin. Lateral means toward the side, away from the midline, and likewise does not mark the far end of a limb.

A.q: What is the imaginary line that runs through the center of the body called?
options: The axis, the central line itself.
Medial, a position close to that line.
Lateral, a position toward the side.
Distal, a point away from an origin.
A.explain: The axis is the imaginary line that runs through the center of the body. Medial names a position close to that line, not the line itself. Lateral names a position toward the side, away from the line. Distal names a point away from the origin of a structure and is not the central line.

A.q: Which term names movement away from the midline of the body?
options: Abduction, movement away from the midline.
Flexion, bending that decreases a joint angle.
Extension, straightening that increases a joint angle.
A.explain: Abduction is movement away from the midline of the body. Adduction is the opposite movement, toward the midline. Flexion is bending that decreases the angle at a joint, and extension is straightening that increases that angle. Neither flexion nor extension is defined by direction relative to the midline.

A.q: What does the term sternalgia mean?
A.explain: Sternalgia is built from Stern/o (sternum) and -algia (pain), so it denotes pain in the sternum, the breastbone. Pain in a tendon would use Ten/o or Tendin/o, as in tenalgia. Inflammation of the sternum would use -itis. Excision of the sternum would use -ectomy.

A.q: Which function belongs to the skeleton and is not a function of muscle contraction?
options: Supporting the body and giving it shape.
A.explain: Support and shape are skeletal functions, along with mineral storage, hemopoiesis, and a surface for muscle attachment. Generating locomotion, producing body heat through contraction, and contracting to move a limb are muscle functions. Protecting internal organs is shared by both systems, so it cannot separate them.

A.q: Which statement about bone tissue is correct?
options: Bone is a dead mineral cast.
Bone is only a nerve tract.
A.explain: Bone is a living structure. It is not a dead mineral cast, not a liquid tissue, and not only a nerve tract. Osteocytes are the specialized connective tissue cells that form it.

A.q: Which pairing of marrow with its product is correct?
options: Red marrow forms blood cells, and yellow marrow is tied to fat, cartilage, and bone production.
Yellow marrow forms blood cells, and red marrow is tied to fat, cartilage, and bone production.
Both marrows form only blood cells, and neither is tied to fat or cartilage.
Both marrows form only fat, and neither forms blood cells.
A.explain: Red marrow produces the blood components, red cells, white cells, and platelets. Yellow marrow is the tissue tied to fats, cartilages, and bone production. At birth all marrow is red, and fat tissue later replaces some of it with yellow marrow. The line that gives blood-cell formation to yellow marrow and fat, cartilage, and bone production to red marrow swaps the two. The line that gives both marrows only blood cells drops the yellow-marrow products. The line that gives both marrows only fat drops blood-cell formation.

A.q: Which function is shared by the skeleton and the muscles?
A.explain: Protecting internal organs is listed for both the skeleton and the muscles, so it is the shared function. Hemopoiesis in red marrow is skeletal. Storing minerals in bone tissue is skeletal. Producing body heat through contraction is muscular.

A.q: Ten/o, tend/o, and tendin/o mean tendon. Which sense is paired with that structure?
A.explain: Tendon is paired with the sense to stretch. To soften is the sense of -malacia, to break is not the tendon gloss, and to record is the sense of -gram. Tenotomy is an incision into a tendon, and tendinitis is inflammation of a tendon.

A.q: What does the term thoracicoabdominal mean?
options: Pertaining to the chest and the abdomen.
Pertaining to the chest and the lower back.
Pertaining to the neck and the arm.
Pertaining to the pelvis and the femur.
A.explain: Thoracicoabdominal is built from Thoracic/o (chest) and the abdomen, so it means pertaining to the chest and the abdomen. Chest and lower back is thoracolumbar. Neck and arm is cervicobrachial. Pelvis and femur is pelvofemoral.

A.q: In cervical myelopathy, the element myel refers to what?
A.explain: Myel/o means bone marrow or the spinal cord, so in cervical myelopathy the myel element names the spinal cord. Muscle is My/o or Muscul/o. Flesh is Sarc/o. Tendon is Ten/o or Tendin/o. Myeloma uses the same form for a bone-marrow tumor.
